source.title: Intent Laundering: AI Safety Datasets Are Not What They Seem

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures harmful-response rates for intent-laundered prompts, but does not test fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, safety-localized weights, causes of token-depth shallowness, or training to deepen safety.
record.gate_note: The 60 rows record the reported ASR comparisons for first-revision intent laundering and the last reported regeneration iteration. These are related safety-bypass results, but use a different attack mechanism from the claim versions, so the rows have versions ["none"]. Dataset word-cloud and duplication analyses do not measure model behaviour. Intermediate regeneration iterations and separate SE/PE results are not extracted; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study rewrites harmful prompts to remove triggering cues (intent laundering) and measures ASR across 10 models. It does no fine-tuning, no per-token KL, no prefilling, suffix or decoding attack, no parameter localization, no cause analysis of token-depth shallowness and no deepening training. The prompt-rewriting attack changes the request, not the response opening, so it does not measure V4's mechanism. The 'shallow' reliance on surface cues it describes is a related but different construct from token-depth shallowness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also conclude that safety alignment built on these datasets likely inherits the same overreliance on triggering cues, and that current alignment is far from robust to real-world threats.
record.recipe_differences: Uses prompt transformation and iterative regeneration, not fine-tuning or token-depth measurement. The paper does not reproduce either original method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by dataset and model; the authors also report higher ASR with further regeneration iterations. They report the first revision as the largest increase.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing overt triggering cues while keeping malicious intent raises mean ASR from 3.86% to 87.54% on AdvBench, from 10.55% to 79.10% on HarmBench, and from 3.54% to 88.06% on StrongREJECT. Iterative regeneration reaches 90–100% ASR across 10 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal in safety-trained models is largely keyed to surface triggering cues in the request rather than to the underlying harmful intent, so cue-free rewrites of harmful requests elicit practical harmful responses.

record.problems: The main ASR tables report no uncertainty estimates. Main safety and practicality outcomes are judged by GPT-5.1; the paper reports agreement with human consensus on a 100-response sample, but that does not provide uncertainty for the main ASRs. The evaluated datasets are 207 AdvBench points, 200 HarmBench points, and 288 StrongREJECT points.
record.rows_left_out: The tables also report separate SE and PE rates and intermediate regeneration stages. The 60-row limit was used for first-revision ASR comparisons and the last reported iteration per model and dataset. Omitted intermediate ASR stages are AdvBench second revision; HarmBench second through fourth revisions; and StrongREJECT second and third revisions (Tables 1–3). Separate SE and PE values were not extracted because ASR is the reported composite attack-success measure.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or aligned-vs-base comparison.
No compliant prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding change; only input prompt rewriting.
No analysis of data or objective causes of token-depth shallowness. The authors argue alignment overrelies on dataset triggering cues, but they argue this, not test it.
No deepening training or its robustness.

record.verdict_notes: The record's rows, baselines and values match Tables 1–3. All rows are correctly linked to none. A state of cannot_determine is acceptable given no version link. Not an original source. ASRs come from a GPT-5.1 judge, which agreed 90% with human consensus on safety across 100 samples. The no-revision ASR uses a different (safety-only) criterion from the revised settings (safety plus practicality), so the baselines are not strictly like-for-like.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or fine-tuning example-count sweep.
No per-token KL or aligned-versus-base distribution comparison.
Tests intent-laundered prompt rewrites, not compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or bypass by getting past opening response tokens.
No weight, rank, or parameter localization.
No test of why safety behaviour is shallow or of data/objective causes of shallowness.
No training to spread safety across response tokens or evaluation of whether such training holds up.
